expectations.text: Output contains a structured comparison table (not just prose)
expectations.evidence: Multiple markdown tables present: startup performance (line 39-43), TypeScript experience (lines 96-101), binary size (lines 116-120), cross-compilation targets (lines 134-142), security model (lines 154-159), CLI libraries (lines 170-177), stability signals (lines 193-200). Well-structured tabular comparisons throughout.

expectations.text: Cites official documentation or official repos as sources
expectations.evidence: Sources section (lines 264-281) lists official documentation URLs including bun.com/docs/bundler/executables, docs.deno.com/runtime/reference/cli/compile/, deno.com/blog/ posts, and GitHub issue #22157 from oven-sh/bun. Inline verification markers also reference official docs (e.g., line 62: 'verified: official docs at bun.com/docs/bundler/executables', line 79: 'verified: official docs at docs.deno.com/runtime/reference/cli/compile').

expectations.text: Covers all three stated criteria: startup speed, TypeScript support, single-binary packaging
expectations.evidence: Dedicated sections for all three: '1. Startup Performance' (lines 35-49), '2. Single-Executable Compilation' (lines 51-90), '3. TypeScript Development Experience' (lines 92-110). Each has detailed comparison, tables, and verdicts.

expectations.text: Provides a clear recommendation with reasoning, not 'both are fine'
expectations.evidence: Line 3 states 'Bun is the stronger choice for this specific use case'. The Recommendation section (lines 210-229) provides a definitive recommendation for Bun with four numbered reasons, plus explicit guidance on when to choose Deno instead and when neither is appropriate.

expectations.text: Does not contain hardcoded tool names like 'Context7', 'WebSearch', or 'WebFetch'
expectations.evidence: Line 144 contains 'context7' (lowercase): '(verified: Bun official docs via context7, Deno official docs via context7)'. While the exact casing 'Context7' is not present, 'context7' is the same tool name and represents leaked internal tool references in the output.

expectations.text: Mentions adoption signals (npm downloads, GitHub stars, release cadence, or similar)
expectations.evidence: Stability & Production Readiness section (lines 193-204) includes: current version numbers and dates (release cadence signal), open issue counts (~4,800 for Bun), LTS policy (Deno's 6-month LTS cycle), backing organizations (Oven Inc, Deno Company). Also references npm compatibility percentages (~95% for Bun). Does not cite raw npm download counts or GitHub star counts, but release cadence and open issue counts qualify as adoption signals.

expectations.text: Does not contain hallucinated/unverifiable factual claims
expectations.evidence: Several claims are questionable: (1) Line 10 states Bun v1.3.10 and Deno v2.7.7 as of March 2026 -- these are future versions that cannot be verified. (2) Line 198 claims 'Anthropic (investment)' as Bun's backing -- there is no publicly known Anthropic investment in Bun/Oven Inc; Bun is backed by Oven Inc. (3) Line 40 cites specific startup times (~8-18ms for Bun, ~40-60ms for Deno) attributed to 'pullflow.com, medium.com/@sonampatel' benchmarks but these exact numbers may not match those sources. (4) The zenn.dev article '9x size reduction' claim (line 124) is acknowledged as not fully verified by the author themselves.

expectations.text: Includes open questions or caveats about what wasn't verified
expectations.evidence: Dedicated sections: 'Open Questions' (lines 254-260) lists 3 explicit open questions (memory usage, native npm packages, long-term maintenance). 'Challenge' section (lines 243-250) identifies the weakest conclusion and lists what wasn't checked (actual binary sizes, memory usage, native npm package behavior). 'Contradictions & Tensions' section (lines 233-239) flags unresolved conflicts in the data.
